claims.text: The starting material is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 produced by conventional powder processing without an oxide dispersion.
Approximately 1–2 vol% nanoscale Y2O3 will be added to the precursor powder before consolidation.
Consolidation of the modified powder will produce a uniform Y2O3 dispersion.
The dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles will localize at grain boundaries and interfaces.
Y2O3 nanoparticles at grain boundaries and interfaces will provide additional sinks for irradiation-induced point defects.
The oxide particles will absorb and annihilate irradiation-induced point defects.
Point-defect absorption by the oxide dispersion will reduce irradiation-induced vacancy supersaturation.
Vacancy supersaturation drives radiation-induced precipitation in this alloy.
Reducing vacancy supersaturation will decrease the density of radiation-induced precipitates.
The Y2O3 dispersion will pin grain boundaries during sintering.
The Y2O3 dispersion will pin grain boundaries during irradiation.
Grain-boundary pinning will improve microstructural stability.
The modified alloy will retain negligible irradiation hardening relative to its pre-irradiation state.
The Y2O3 addition will enhance sinterability and thereby improve suitability for practical bulk fabrication.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 develops detectable precipitates after approximately 8 dpa at 700–900 °C.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits negligible irradiation hardening under the stated irradiation conditions.
The predicted behavior is limited to energetic-particle irradiation up to approximately 8 dpa at 700–900 °C.
Existing data are limited for oxide dispersions in this specific W-Ta-Cr-V alloy under high-dose irradiation.
